draft.title: The women's movement in Australia
card: From the 1960s, women in Australia campaigned for equal treatment at work. Many used protests, unions, lobbying and court cases.
Equal pay
Women were often paid less than men for the same work. The Arbitration Commission made decisions in 1969 and 1972 that moved Australia toward equal pay.
Marriage bar
Married women had been barred from permanent jobs in the Commonwealth public service. The campaign to end this ban succeeded in 1966.
Sex Discrimination Act
The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 made it unlawful to treat people unfairly because of their sex. It covers areas such as work, and later reforms built on it.
draft.remember: Women's campaigns led to equal pay decisions, the end of the marriage bar and a law against sex discrimination.

a.q: Before the marriage bar ended, what rule applied to women in the Commonwealth public service?
opts: Married women could not hold permanent jobs
Women could not be paid any wage at all
Women could only work in unions
Married women had to be paid more than men
a.why: The marriage bar stopped married women from keeping permanent public service jobs, so many had to resign when they married. It was about who could hold a job, not about wages alone.
a.clue: The bar was linked to a woman's marital status.

b.q: Priya is a clerk in Parramatta in 1990. Her manager pays her less than a male clerk because she is a woman. Which law makes this unlawful?
opts: The Sex Discrimination Act 1984
The 1969 equal pay decision alone
The ban on married women in public service jobs
The 1972 decision on marriage
b.why: The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 made unfair treatment because of sex unlawful, which covers Priya's case. The ban on married women was a rule that was ended, not a protection, so it does not apply.
b.clue: Look for the law passed in the 1980s about unfair treatment because of sex.

a.best: Married women could not hold permanent jobs

proposal.title: The women's movement in Australia
card: From the 1960s, women in Australia campaigned for equal treatment at work. They used protests, unions, lobbying and cases before the Arbitration Commission, which set wages.
Equal pay

Women were often paid less than men. In 1969 the Arbitration Commission granted equal pay for equal work, and in 1972 it widened this to equal pay for work of equal value. Both decisions were about pay rates.
Marriage bar
Married women had been barred from permanent jobs in the Commonwealth public service, so many had to resign when they married. The campaign to end this ban succeeded in 1966.
Sex Discrimination Act
The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 made it unlawful to treat people unfairly because of their sex. It covers areas such as work, including hiring and promotion, and education.
proposal.remember: Women's campaigns won equal pay decisions, ended the marriage bar and gained a law against sex discrimination.

a.q: Before 1966, why did many women in the Commonwealth public service resign when they married?
opts: Married women were barred from permanent jobs
The 1969 equal pay decision required it
The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 required it
Married women had to be paid more than men
a.why: The marriage bar stopped married women from holding permanent public service jobs, so many had to leave when they married. The equal pay decision and the Sex Discrimination Act came after 1966, and both aimed to make treatment fairer, not to push women out.
a.clue: Check the dates: what was in place before 1966?

b.q: In 1990, Priya, who is single, works for a Sydney company. Her manager refuses to promote her because she is a woman. Which reform made this unlawful?
opts: The Sex Discrimination Act 1984
The 1972 equal pay decision
The 1969 equal pay decision
The end of the marriage bar in 1966
b.why: The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 made unfair treatment because of sex unlawful at work, including in promotion. The equal pay decisions are tempting, but they set pay rates and did not cover promotion. The marriage bar was about married women in the public service.
b.clue: Priya's problem is not about her pay rate or her marriage.
